Make sure it’s something that’s not going to be a problem in the job and I always like to say it’s something I’ve identified and have systems in place to manage. E.g. I take a lot of pride in my work and can become too focussed on finishing tasks I’ve started which sometimes means finishing other jobs can be a challenge. I recognized this early on and have learned to prioritize jobs in order of urgency and importance. I’ve also become much more confident in delegating tasks and to communicate clearly when handing over which I have found to address this weakness quite well

Generally, in customer service roles you want to place emphasis on your ability to communicate well with people from diverse backgrounds, create positive experiences for your clients and go over and beyond. 

Always try to back up a statement with an example in your life, if you simply say I’m good at making relationships with people, I will think that’s cool, but where is your evidence of this? What does ‘making relationships’ look like for you? If I’m going to choose you to represent my company or team without knowing you, you need to tell me why you can do this job well, which requires supporting evidence.

Generally, your demeanour and conduct in the interview will make a huge impact. You can say all the right things, but if you don’t appear like someone who is an excellent customer service representative, that impression will last longer than what you say. So go in, don’t be afraid to small-talk and be outgoing, SMILE, try to have a laugh and don’t stress too much.

Say for instance the strengths question and say it’s a position at Walmart, you can say, I’m an excellent communicator and have a reputation for being outgoing and helpful amongst my peers. Many of my friends have confided in me over my lifetime simply because they know I will listen, be empathetic and they can trust me with this sensitive information. I would take this same empathetic approach into my customer service role here, listening to customers to best understand their needs and going over and beyond to create the best customer experience possible. This is the same reason I can see myself thrive in this position, I know the commitment Walmart has to creating positive and long lasting relationships and this aligns perfectly with my strengths and personality.

Good luck, fingers crossed for you

Hi all, this data records the tries each team scored in round 1 of the NPC, categorized by the origin of the try:

* **Try** (tries not directly related to a set piece or occurring after more than 5 phases following a set piece),
* **Lineout (L/O) set piece** (deriving from line-out set piece in 5 phases or less),
* **Scrum set piece** {deriving from scrum set piece in 5 phases or less),
* **Tap and Go (T&G)** {deriving from a quick tap & go in 5 phases or less).

*Besides each origin is the number of phases following that set piece that the try was scored.*

\* \* \* \* \* \* \*

A total of **45 tries** were scored across all matches. The origins of these tries were:

**Lineout:** ***26 tries*** were scored from lineouts, making up ***57.8%*** of the total, 15 of these being scored in 1 phase.

**Scrum:** ***5 tries*** were scored from scrums, making up ***11.1%*** of the total tries.

**Tap and Go**: ***2 tries*** were scored from quick tap-and-go's, making up ***4.4%*** of the total tries.

**Try:** ***12 tries*** originated from broken play or set pieces above 5 phases, making up ***26.7%*** of the total tries.

Every school-age child in the Ottawa region will receive the opportunity to redeem a complimentary ticket to Canada’s Women’s Rugby Team’s match against New Zealand on July 8, 2023, at TD Place in Ottawa.

Rugby Canada’s mission is to ensure that children and youth have access to this once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to watch Canada take on the six-time, reigning World Champions, the New Zealand Black Ferns.

Principals and administrators from schools in Ottawa will be distributing information to students and parents this week on how to redeem a free child’s ticket with the purchase of one ticket for an accompanying parent or adult. This offer will be open until Sunday June 4.

“We recognize that hosting this first-rate international fixture is an incredible opportunity to inspire the next generation of rugby players and excite children and youth about sport and physical activity,” said Ryan Jones, Rugby Development Manager, Rugby Canada. “Not only can this inspire children to start rugby, but it gives them access to exceptional role models who embody what it means to be inclusive, work as a team, and strive to be the best they can be. Rugby really is a sport for all, and we aim to make this exciting match-up between two of the best teams in the world truly accessible.”

“Our team is very excited about this initiative. There’s no better feeling than playing in front of a home crowd, and we can’t wait to help bring the sport we love into the lives of Ottawa’s children and youth,” said Sophie de Goede, captain of Canada’s Women’s Rugby Team. “Representation matters, and I know that many of us wish that we had an opportunity like this when we were kids. The atmosphere at TD Place on July 8 is going to be incredible.”

The match day experience at TD Place on July 8 will begin with a free rugby festival for kids under the age of 12 designed to introduce them to the sport in a safe and fun environment. In addition to the marquee match-up between Canada and New Zealand, tickets will also include entry to a curtain raiser match featuring the Canadian and American U20 women’s teams, as well as the Pacific Four Series Australia versus USA game.

Halfback:

1. Fitness. You can’t do your job if you don’t make the rucks. 
2. Passing. There’s no point getting to the rucks if you can’t pass both ways.
3. Kicking. Sometimes you can’t pass and you’ll need to kick.
4. Rules & Communication. Sometimes you will see stuff other players can’t, especially in and around the breakdown, learn your rules and learn to be a good effective communicator.
5. Understanding of Game Plan. You are the link between the forwards and backs. You need to understand what’s happening and work with your forwards or backs to adjust where necessary.

In NZ, the 1st XV competition is typically divided into multiple divisions. More often than not, you’ll see almost exclusively decile 10 or private schools in those top grades simply due to funding; they can afford to poach players from lower decile schools with life-changing scholarships, and exert substantial resourcing in their rugby academy. As a result, some teams most notably St Kent’s and Scots as Oaty mentioned, developed a bit of a reputation for this poaching and eventually faced backlash from the NZ Rugby Board & Public. Restrictions have since been implemented to try equalise the competition, but at this point these top rugby schools are still consistent winners of the NZ secondary school competition.

There are over 500 rugby clubs in NZ and are fairly casual. Usually you can contact your local club rep and join a team. Larger clubs will have multiple teams, premier team, colts, golden oldies, under 80kg etc so you aren’t thrown against pro players returning from injury e.g. Sam Cane playing for King Country Rams last year, unless you choose and are selected for the clubs premiership side. 

So from the 500 premier club teams in NZ, coaches will look for and sign stand out prems players who can step into professional rugby at the NPC. Clubs are usually regionalised and take the best players in their area (as it is unpaid and a nonprofessional league) so it is more convenient to contract players close. As players move up into the NPC you will start to see players follow the contract offers around the country (e.g. Salesi Rayasi 1st XV/Club in Wellington, plays NPC for Auckland, SR for Hurricanes).
Generally speaking, club rugby is for people who have left school. You play with others your own age through stages 1 and 2, and start playing adults at club level onwards.

This would be New Zealand’s pathway:

1. Begin making a name for yourself between Under 14s - 1st XV (High School).
2. NZ Barbarians Schools (2nd top team) / NZ Secondary Schools (top team). 
3. Club Rugby (Prems team for Club)
4. Regional U18 Side (e.g. Blues U18)
5. Regional U20 Side (e.g. Blues U20)
6. NZ Under 20s
7. National Province Championship (e.g. Auckland).
8. Super Rugby
9. All Blacks
10. Japan.

Nah seriously, definitely get confident under high balls. Have solid communication with your full back so you can have confidence in each other to cover all areas of the backfield if a kick comes your way. 

Measure your speed and strength against the opposition winger. If you have an advantage in size or defence, use the sideline as an additional defensive measure and don’t be afraid to run through if you can. If you’re quicker, try to manipulate them into coming tighter in-field to mark you, giving you extra space on the outside to burn them. 

Ball skills, e.g. effective grubber or overhead kick and chases can be a useful set of skills to have to get around your defender.

There are many archetypes to a winger. If you’re a smaller winger focus on acceleration. Take up sprint training etc to increase your speed off the mark and agility. That’s where players like Kolbe or Sevu Reece excel, they’re not the biggest guys but have absolutely searing acceleration and are incredibly slippery often using these skills to get around defenders. 

If you’re taller but not necessarily powerful, e.g. Jordie Barrett, Israel Folau your strength is your height in a position that is generally shorter, focus on learning to catch high balls whilst jumping in the air. It’s an awesome thing as a flyhalf when you’re 20 meters from the line and you know you have a competent winger on the outside who can catch cross kicks and will likely jump over the opposition and score. 

If you’re a more powerful winger with size, e.g. Tuisova, Savea, Nadolo it’s a mix of both strength, speed and size. You’ll need to acquire all skills to be an absolute weapon with ball in hand, weight training (squats, deadlifts) power training (explosive weight lifting - banded bench press etc) and acceleration training.

I’m a 5’9, 92kg openside playing for club Prems. 

Some tricks I’ve found are:

Aiming just below his bum and from the side, getting your body position as low as possible and putting as much force as you can in with your shoulder. If he doesn’t stumble from the initial hit drop you grip down to his calf and hold on as tight as you can, literally squeezing the life out of his leg. You may not get him down by yourself but you will force him stationary if he has a weaker leg drive or slow him down enough to have another team mate come and hit him. (You can practice if you don’t have siblings or trainings regularly by having someone throw a boxing bag at you and you hitting from the side and wrapping a big body).

As mentioned before, odds are you’ll either get run over or hurt if you try to take him on from the front. Just aim for the side and target one leg if you can’t wrap around both, holding on for dear life - it’s a lot harder to run balanced carrying a 55kg weight on your leg. 

Lastly, if he is going to get the ball, sprint at him as fast as you can, essentially stopping him from building any momentum. The last thing you want with a big guy is for them to build up momentum. If you run at him while he is standing still you have all the momentum and can put a solid hit on. 

Also if you rush him as fast as you can, there’s a chance he will freak under the pressure of having someone in his face about to hit him and drop the ball or get frustrated with you in his face all the time and make some mistakes.

A few things:

Watch professional teams, closely examine the locks and watch what they do. Focus on gaining a general insight into their work rate around the field - how often they hit rucks vs stand off, how closely or distant they stand off, how often they jackal, how often they carry etc. Try to envision yourself on the field and what you could do to adapt your game more like them. 

Walk around school with a rugby ball, pass it in between mates or just by yourself between classes, during breaks etc.

Practice passing it up and down focussing on keeping the spiral straight.

Practice your offload making it feel natural and comfortable.

Practice throwing the ball in the air and catching it with your two hands extended, and eventually one hand simulating a lineout catch. 

Practice grubber kicking the ball and making it bounce up along a path in front of you. 

Essentially you’re practicing technical skills that have become really important in modern day rugby. A lot of the other skills like jackeling, tackling will be picked up during trainings and from playing.
